newsitem.title: BRAZIL: YEAREND-Selloffs seen buoying Brazil stocks in '97.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND-Selloffs seen buoying Brazil stocks in '97.

text.p: Brazilian stocks, while unlikely to repeat this year's spectacular run-up, will post strong gains in 1997, boosted by privatizations and progress on economic and government reforms, analysts said.
"The perspective is very positive," said Luciano Camargo, head of equities sales for ING Barings' local unit.
"Brazil is going to be a very good option. Things are on track," he added.
Local shares surged this year on the back of Brazil's economic recovery, currency stability, a consumer spending boom fueled by low inflation and healthy rises in stock prices worldwide.
So far in 1996, the Sao Paulo bourse's Bovespa index .BVSP of the 49 most-traded shares has jumped by about 55 percent to more than 66,550 points, with benchmark Telebras rising even further.
STOCKS TO RIDE SELLOFF WAVE UPWARD

Market experts said bolsa prices are expected to continue rising in 1997 though at a slower clip. State telecoms and electrical firms, headed for the auction block and likely to enjoy revenue boosts from expected rate adjustments, possess the best upside potential.
"Our view is that state-owned companies are going to drive the market in '97," said asset manager Saulo Holzman of BBA Capital.
Analysts said the Bovespa is likely to surge to at least 80,000 points by year's end, or 20 percent over current levels and a nearly 100-percent run-up in two years, they said.

Slated to start next year are the break-up and sale of giant Telebras, Latin America's largest telecom, and the sell-off of Sao Paulo state's power companies. Billions of dollars in foreign investment are expected to flow into the economy as a result of the privatizations.
"1997 will be the year of the electric companies," said Vital Menezes, head of sales and trading at German bank Deutsche Morgan Grenfell's local unit.
Strong showings are expected from Minas Gerais state's Cemig Paulo's soon-to-be-privatized CPFL, Cesp and Eletropaulo, he said.

Moreover, the market will be watching closely the outcome of Tuesday's sale of a 35-percent stake in Rio Grande do Sul's Companhia Riograndense de Telecomunicacoes to see what foreign investors are willing to pay for a Brazilian telecom.
Also contributing to the generally upbeat climate for local stocks are expectations of deepening reforms on the fiscal, pension and administrative fronts.
RE-ELECTION BILL CRUCIAL

Analysts, however, say progress on these issues, and to a lesser degree privatization, hinges on the success of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's bid to amend the constitution to allow him to stand for re-election in 1998.
"Everything will depend on re-election," one trader said. "The privatization process looks irreversible, but it would be much better with Fernando Henrique in command."
"We're not favorable on the retails and white goods because of the credit problems and more competition," said Holzman, noting food and beverage stocks looked more appetizing.
"We like (brewer) Brahma and (meat producer) Perdigao," he said. "That kind of consumption does not suffer from a credit crunch."

Mining, steel, paper and pulp and petrochemical stocks in general are seen underperforming the market. "There are some interesting stories there but I wouldn't build up a portfolio on them," Holzman said.

While Brasilia plans to privatize state mining giant Companhia Vale do Rio Doce, the stock is not attractive, he said. "I don't like Vale because I think it's too pricey. And the way they structured the privatization model doesn't benefit the minority shareholder," he added.
-- Sao Paulo newsroom 5511 248 5413
Meanwhile, projections for only moderate economic growth in 1997 have some bolsa-watchers pessimistic about private company stocks, some of which posted sharp gains this year.

"We see economic growth at four percent in Brazil next year but some see it at 3.5 percent," Menezes said, adding that such levels were not enough to sustain this year's upward momentum in private company stocks.
RETAIL TO WANE, FOOD MORE APPETIZING
One such sector is retail, whose prices soared this year but began to flatten recently ahead of speculation about new credit restrictions to curb import demand.
